title: Trump defends tariffs at rally as he touts new US Audi plant
article:
(Oct 25): US President Donald Trump defended his decision to wield tariffs during a campaign rally in Georgia, saying they’ve made the US richer as he announced that Volkswagen AG agreed to build a new US$4.2 billion Audi plant in the state.

“Think of that. 200,000 cars a year. That’s incredible,” Trump told a crowd in the city of Perry. “This will be the single largest investment in US auto industry history, modern history.”

Later, he added, “Without tariffs, they wouldn’t be coming in.”

Trump was speaking as Republicans are trying to flip a Senate seat held by Democrat Jon Ossoff in the midterm elections, despite trailing in the polls.

The campaign stop marked Trump’s second in the state in as many weeks, an indication of the importance of the Senate contest in Georgia.

With less than two weeks until Election Day on Nov 3, though, Representative Mike Collins, the Republican candidate, faces an uphill battle in a state that was once a GOP stronghold. The RealClearPolitics average of polls has Ossoff leading by more than eight percentage points, while the nonpartisan Cook Political Report has forecast the race as “likely Democrat.”

See also: Nippon Steel raises US mill upgrade to US$3 bil as costs climb

That dynamic is indicative of a broader political climate that has soured for Republican candidates. Trump is at historic low approval ratings and his efforts to tout manufacturing investment promises have failed to resonate with voters who are more concerned with high costs of living and wage growth. The war in Iran has also spiked energy prices, adding further strain to household budgets.

The Audi announcement marks a political win for Trump, who has been on the defensive about the domestic effects of his tariffs, particularly on inflation, in a number of battleground Senate races.

Bloomberg News reported earlier that Volkswagen plans to manufacture the Audi Q7, Q8 and Q9 models at the Georgia plant, according to a US official involved in the talks.

See also: Rio Tinto and China state buyer agree deal on iron ore supplies — Bloomberg

Volkswagen will also expand its Scout Motors plant under construction in Blythewood, South Carolina, adding 25,000 units per year of capacity for a model yet to be determined, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to detail the plans.

Audi said in a news release that the US$4 billion plant would create some 4,500 jobs with an annual capacity of up to 200,000 vehicles. Construction will begin next year, with the aim of beginning vehicle production in the early 2030s.

“We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” Audi chairman of the Board of Management Gernot Döllner said at the rally, standing near Trump. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.”

Richard Motes, 61, a Perry resident who used to work at an aircraft manufacturer, praised the Audi plant announcement.

“That’s awesome, I want jobs to come to Georgia,” Motes said.

“I’m dead red,” he added. “If they let me push a button to vote all Republican, I’d push the button.”

Trump has been travelling nearly daily in the run-up to the midterms, seeking to help boost Republicans in competitive races across the country. Polls indicate Democrats are likely to regain control of the House, but the Senate is still in play with Republicans on the defensive in unexpected states such as Texas and Ohio.

Another rally attendee, Chris Capp, 55, a former Army National Guard employee, said he’s 50-50 on whether Trump is still an asset to Republican candidates in Georgia, given his falling popularity.

“I love Trump to death, but sometimes he should keep his mouth shut,” he said.

Georgia is also home to a a competitive governor’s race between Democratic candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson, which the Cook report has rated a toss-up.

Former US president Barack Obama is expected to campaign in Georgia with Ossoff and Bottoms on Wednesday. While Ossoff has pledged to serve a full six-year Senate term if reelected, he’s been seen as a potential Democratic 2028 contender.

Trump won Georgia in 2024 and 2016, but lost to former president Joe Biden in 2020, prompting the president to promote unfounded theories of fraud in that election. Trump pressured Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to “find” the votes he needed to win the state. Trump and allies were indicted to face allegations of carrying out election interference, but those charges were eventually dropped.

The president has repeatedly promoted false claims that he won the 2020 election and questioned the integrity of Georgia’s voting counting. Raffensperger earlier this month told Bloomberg Television that he expects the state’s election results by midnight on Election Day, downplaying the president’s remarks.

title: Sinking profits turn China’s US$3.5 tril stock rout into trap
article:
(Oct 25): Pessimism has gripped Chinese stocks, with no end in sight for a deepening selloff as investors confront the realities of an economy that’s weak enough to erode corporate profits but not to trigger forceful new stimulus.

The world’s second-largest equities market has lost US$3.5 trillion in value from a peak in May, data compiled by Bloomberg show. The rout intensified last week, pushing the onshore benchmark CSI 300 Index into a bear market and a technology sector gauge in Hong Kong toward erasing all its gains since Beijing’s sweeping growth support package two years ago.

At the heart of investor gloom is an unsettling realization that a protracted consumption slump and the race-to-the-bottom mentality among businesses is taking a heavier toll on earnings across industries from banks to electric car makers and AI model developers. Further darkening the outlook is the growing perception that Chinese leaders are in no rush to jump-start an economy that is slowing but at a tolerable speed.

“It is too early to conclude that the worst is over,” said Ulrich Urbahn, head of multi-asset strategy and research at Berenberg. “The biggest concern remains profitability: China’s strength in production and exports is not translating consistently into stronger domestic demand, pricing power and corporate earnings.”

The third-quarter reporting season got off a disappointing start, with battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology Co Ltd, or CATL, suffering a profit miss that was symptomatic of both weak demand and fierce competition.

See also: Chery eyes producing cars in Canada as Chinese automakers circle the US

The consensus 2026 earnings forecasts for the MSCI China Index members has declined by over 4% since the end of March, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The Hang Seng Tech Index, dominated by Chinese Internet firms mired in e-commerce price wars, has seen profit projections plunge more than 13% during the period.

Yet even against the lowered expectations, the MSCI China’s constituents that have released results have missed consensus forecasts by an average of 9%, set for the second worst quarterly miss in two years, according to Bloomberg calculations.

See also: China's US$150 bil AI model stock slump shows no sign of easing

Among them, AI infrastructure builder China Mobile Ltd’s January-September net profit tumbled 8% on year amid cost pressures, while major materials firm Ganfeng Lithium Group Co also missed estimates on falling prices.

“CATL is the best poster child of what’s going on: great innovative company that’s doing great things but a victim of cut-throat competition and margin squeeze,” said Jason Lemire, chief investment officer at Bold Wealth Partners. “Competition is encouraged and generally brutal in China, not shareholder friendly.”

The earnings pressure has left companies, particularly China’s Internet behemoths that are in a tense race to fund costly AI infrastructure build-outs, increasingly out of cash. That has forced some of them to tap the equities market to raise funds, such as Alibaba Group Holding Ltd’s US$10 billion follow-on stock sale, which further diluted share value.

“I’d always weigh Japan, Korea and Taiwanese firms over China because they have better earnings,” said Stanley Tang, senior portfolio manager at Sumitomo Mitsui DS Asset Management. “If you ask me what China can do, hard to think of any — even further localisation of tech may not help to boost share prices.”

Weakening investor confidence is also showing up via other measures. Turnover in China’s onshore stock market is hovering near the lowest level since July last year, while the outstanding amount of margin trades — bets funded by borrowed cash — fell to the least in a year.

To be sure, the slumping market has already prompted authorities to mobilise state funds known as the national team to prevent stock prices from spiralling out of control.

Meanwhile, the recent rout has boosted the appeal of Chinese equities to some investors. Bridgewater Associates’ China arm, for one, said it has turned “prudently optimistic” on local stocks, saying the declines in the third quarter were largely driven by liquidity while valuations aren’t high. It also argued that policy favors long-term capital formation and more money may flow into equities given low bond yields. Still, skepticism abounds that while the national team’s rescue efforts may be a temporary fix, the market’s long-term prospect remains dim given policymakers’ reluctance to adopt big-bang stimulus measures to accelerate economic growth.

China’s third-quarter gross domestic product grew 4.5% from a year ago, nudging expansion in the first nine months back into the government’s annual goal of 4.5%-5%. That target-meeting performance has given authorities more reason to stick to a drip-feed style of growth support, without compromising fiscal discipline or further reducing historically low borrowing costs.

“Policymakers are comfortable with the nature of economic growth,” said William Bratton, head of cash equity research for Asia Pacific at BNP Paribas. “As a result, either because they’re consciously keeping it in reserve or because philosophically they don’t believe in it, there’s no urgency to use fiscal measures to promote large scale consumption.”
